The Elements of Art & Color Theory 🎨

Every painting, poster, doodle, and video game is built from the same basic building blocks. Learn them here — then jump into your own studio and create.

✏️ Warm-up · Loosen your drawing hand

Scroll down to your studio (or grab paper) and do each one quickly — messy is fine, it's just a warm-up:

  • Draw 5 circles as fast as you can
  • Draw one wavy line all the way across
  • Draw a square, a triangle, and a star
  • Make a fade from light to dark — press softly, then harder

🧱 The 7 Elements of Art

ElementWhat it isSpot it in real life
LineA mark with length and directionThe edge of a phone, your signature
ShapeA flat, enclosed area (2-D)A road sign, an emoji
FormA shape with depth (3-D)A basketball, a sculpture
ColorHue made by reflected lightA sunset, a paint set
ValueHow light or dark something isShadows on a face
TextureHow a surface feels (or looks like it feels)Tree bark, soft fur
SpaceThe area around and between objectsThe gap that makes a drawing look far away
💡
Memory trick: "Little Sharks Find Colorful Vivid Textured Spaces." = Line, Shape, Form, Color, Value, Texture, Space.

Value: the secret weapon

Value is how light or dark a color is. Shading light-to-dark makes a flat circle look like a 3-D ball:

🌈 Color Theory Basics

The color wheel

  • Primary colors — red, yellow, blue. Can't be mixed from others.
  • Secondary colors — orange, green, purple. Mix two primaries.
  • Complementary colors sit opposite (like blue & orange). Side by side, they pop!

Warm vs. Cool

Warm 🔥 reds, oranges, yellows — cozy, exciting, close.
Cool ❄️ blues, greens, purples — calm, quiet, far away.

Use everything you learned. Follow the steps in your studio — take your time. 🎨

  1. Draw a straight horizon line across the middle (the Line element).
  2. Add a big round sun in a warm color (red, orange, yellow).
  3. Fill the sky with a cool complementary color (blue or purple) so the sun pops.
  4. Show value: darker sky at the top, lighter near the sun.
  5. Add texture to the ground — short strokes for grass, or waves for water.

Shading & Form: Make It Look 3-D ✏️

In Lesson 1 you met value. Now you'll use it to turn flat shapes into round, solid forms that pop off the page.

🎯 Today's plan

  • How a light source creates highlights and shadows
  • The 5 parts of light and shadow on a 3-D object
  • How to shade a sphere step by step
  • A studio challenge: make a flat circle look like a solid ball
  • 1. Warm-up
  • 2. Light & shadow
  • 3. Shading a form
  • 4. Studio challenge
  • 5. Quick check

✏️ Warm-up · Build a value scale

In the studio below, draw a row of 5 boxes and fill them from white → light gray → gray → dark gray → black. Smooth, even steps — this trains your eye for shading.

  • My 5 boxes go evenly from lightest to darkest
  • No big jumps between steps

💡 Light & Shadow

Pick a light source (say, a lamp on the left). Everything facing the light is bright; everything turned away is dark. On a round object you'll see 5 areas:

PartWhat it is
HighlightThe brightest spot, where light hits most directly
LightThe lit side, a medium-light value
Core shadowThe darkest band, on the edge turning away from the light
Reflected lightA faint glow on the shadow side, bounced from the table
Cast shadowThe dark shape the object throws onto the table
💡
Key idea: the core shadow is not at the very edge — there's a thin strip of reflected light beyond it. That little detail is what makes objects look real.

🟠 Shading a Sphere — step by step

  1. Lightly draw a circle and decide where the light comes from.
  2. Leave a small white highlight on the light side.
  3. Add a core shadow as a curved band on the opposite side.
  4. Blend the light area smoothly between the highlight and the core shadow.
  5. Soften a sliver of reflected light just past the core shadow.
  6. Drop a cast shadow on the ground, darkest right under the ball.

Try it — label the shading

The brightest spot is the . The darkest band on the object is the . The dark shape on the table is the .

Use the grays below. Pick a light direction and shade a circle using all 5 parts. Don't rush — build the dark up slowly. Hit 💾 Save when you're proud of it.

One-Point Perspective: Draw 3-D Space 📐

Perspective is the trick that makes a flat page look deep — like you could step right into it. It all starts with a single dot.

🎯 Today's plan

  • What a horizon line and vanishing point are
  • How orthogonal lines pull everything toward that point
  • Draw a 3-D box in one-point perspective
  • Build a scene in your studio
  • 1. Warm-up
  • 2. Perspective basics
  • 3. Draw a box
  • 4. Studio challenge
  • 5. Quick check

✏️ Warm-up · Set the stage

In the studio below, do this fast:

  • Draw one straight horizon line across the middle
  • Put a single dot on it — the vanishing point
  • Draw 5 lines that all start at the dot and spread out like sun rays

📐 Perspective Basics

TermWhat it is
Horizon lineThe line at your eye level, where sky meets ground
Vanishing pointThe dot on the horizon where everything shrinks to nothing
Orthogonal linesThe slanted lines that run from an object back to the vanishing point
💡
Objects look bigger up close and smaller as they near the vanishing point — that shrinking is what your eye reads as depth.

📦 Draw a Box in 3-D

  1. Draw a horizon line with a vanishing point on it.
  2. Draw a square off to one side — the front of the box.
  3. Lightly connect each corner of the square to the vanishing point.
  4. Mark the back of the box with a smaller square along those lines.
  5. Trace the real edges, erase the extras — a solid 3-D cube!

Try it — name the part

The dot everything shrinks toward is the , the line at eye level is the , and the slanted lines to the dot are .

🖌️ Studio Challenge · A room in perspective

Draw the inside of a room: a small square for the back wall, then connect its corners out to a vanishing point to make the floor, ceiling and side walls. Add a door or window, then 💾 Save.

Tints, Shades & Color Mood 🎨

Take any color and you can make it softer or deeper — and change the whole feeling of a picture. Use your new blending wheel to try it!

  • How colors set a mood

🎨 Warm-up · Mix it

Color + white makes a , color + black makes a , color + gray makes a .

🌗 Tints, Shades & Tones

MixWhat you getExample
Color + whiteA tint — lighter, softerRed → pink
Color + blackA shade — darker, deeperRed → maroon
Color + grayA tone — calmer, mutedRed → dusty rose
🎡
On your blending wheel below, the slider on the side makes any color lighter or darker — that's tints and shades in action!

😊 Color & Mood

Colors make us feel things — artists use that on purpose.

  • Warm + bright (red, orange, yellow) → energetic, happy, exciting
  • Cool + pale (soft blue, green) → calm, peaceful, gentle
  • Dark shades → serious, mysterious, or moody

Form & Shading: Drawing in 3D 🎨

Today you turn flat shapes into solid objects that look like you could pick them up. The trick is light and shadow — and you already know tints and shades from last time, so you're ready. Take your time: this one is a real 45 minutes of drawing.

🎯 Today's plan (about 45 minutes)

  • Warm-up — turn flat shapes into solid forms
  • Learn the 5 parts of light on any object
  • Build a value scale and read light direction
  • Studio A: shade a 3D sphere with your blending wheel
  • Studio B: a tiny still-life of solid shapes with cast shadows
  • Quick check + a short reflection
  • 1. Warm-up
  • 2. 5 parts of light
  • 3. Value & direction
  • 4. Studio A
  • 5. Studio B
  • 6. Check

🟡 Warm-up · Flat → Solid

Every solid object is built from a simple form. A flat shape is 2D (just an outline); a form is the same thing made 3D with shading. Match each flat shape to the form it becomes:

A flat circle becomes a , a flat square becomes a , and a flat triangle becomes a .

💡
Artists draw the simple form first (a light circle, a light box) and then shade it. The shading is what makes your eye believe it's solid.

💡 The 5 parts of light on any object

Pick one light direction (say, top-left) and every round object shows these five things, always in the same order from bright to dark:

#PartWhat it is
1HighlightThe tiny brightest dot where light hits straight on
2MidtoneThe object's normal, medium color
3Core shadowThe darkest band, curving across the side away from the light
4Reflected lightA soft glow on the shadow edge, bounced up from the table
5Cast shadowThe dark shape the object throws onto the ground

Test yourself: the brightest spot is the , the dark band wrapping the form is the , and the shadow on the table is the .

🌑🌕 Value scale & light direction

A value scale is a strip that steps from white to black. Drawing one trains your hand to make smooth, believable shadows. In your head, read this 5-step scale from lightest to darkest:

  • ⚪ White
  • 🌑 Light gray
  • 🌘 Medium gray
  • 🌑 Dark gray
  • ⚫ Black

If the light comes from the top-left, the highlight sits on the side, and the core shadow + cast shadow fall toward the side. The shadow is always on the side .

🎡
This is where last lesson pays off: on the blending wheel, slide up for the highlight (a tint) and down for the core and cast shadows (shades) — same color, different value.

🖌️ Studio A · Shade a 3D sphere

Let's make a flat circle look like a real ball. Work in this order:

  • 1. Pick a color on the wheel and lightly fill a big circle (that's your midtone).
  • 2. Slide the side bar down for a darker shade and paint the core shadow as a curved band on the lower-right.
  • 3. Slide up for a light tint and dab a highlight on the upper-left.
  • 4. Switch to ink/black and paint a cast shadow on the ground, stretching to the lower-right.
  • 5. Save it when you're proud of it!
20px

🍎 Studio B · A tiny still-life

Now use the same trick on a little scene. Draw two or three solid objects sitting on a table — maybe a ball, a box, and a cup — and give each one a highlight, a core shadow, and a cast shadow that all point the same direction (because there's one light). Matching shadow directions is the secret that makes a drawing look real.

📏
Composition tip — the rule of thirds: imagine the canvas split into 9 squares by two lines across and two down. Place your main object near a spot where the lines cross, not dead-center. It instantly looks more interesting.
14px

Drawing Faces: Portrait Proportions ✏️

Faces look hard until you know the secret: every face follows the same simple measuring rules. Learn the rules, then spend most of today drawing one real, careful portrait.

🎯 Today’s plan (about 30 minutes)

  • Learn the 5 proportion rules of a face (~6 min)
  • Warm-up: place the features in the right spots (~4 min)
  • Studio: draw and shade one careful face (~16 min)
  • Quick check + reflection (~4 min)
  • 1. Rules
  • 2. Warm-up
  • 3. Studio
  • 4. Check

📏 The 5 rules of face proportion

RuleWhere it goes
1. EyesHalfway down the head — not near the top (beginners always draw them too high)
2. Eye spacingThere is room for one more eye between the two eyes
3. Bottom of noseHalfway between the eyes and the chin
4. MouthAbout one-third of the way down from the nose to the chin
5. EarsTop lines up with the eyebrows, bottom with the bottom of the nose
💡
The biggest fix for beginner faces: drop the eyes to the middle of the head. The forehead is bigger than you think!

🟡 Warm-up · Where does it go?

Fill each blank from what you just learned.

The eyes sit the head. Between the two eyes there is room for . The bottom of the nose is halfway between the eyes and the , and the ears line up with the eyebrows and the .

🎨 Studio · Draw a face with the guides

Lightly draw an oval. Then use the rules above to place the features. Use the blending wheel to mix a skin tone, then shade one side a little darker (that's your form shadow from Lesson 5!). Take the full time on this — a careful face is the whole 30 minutes.

Composition: The Principles of Design 🎨

You’ve learned the building blocks (line, value, colour, form). The principles of design are the rules for arranging those blocks so a picture feels balanced and grabs the eye. Real artists plan with these on purpose.

🧭 How this lesson works — read this first

This is a big one, so here’s the plan. Do the sections in order, top to bottom:

  • Read each coloured box first — it teaches and shows you how.
  • Drop-downs (▾): pick the one correct word.
  • ☑ Select-all boxes: tick every correct one, leave the wrong ones empty.
  • Type-in boxes: work it out (scratch paper / calculator is fine) and type the answer.
  • Press the Check buttons to see green (right) and red (wrong).
📊
Watch the bar at the very top — it fills as you finish. Keep going until it says “Lesson complete!” That’s how you know you really did the whole thing.

🎯 Today’s plan

  • Learn 6 principles: balance, contrast, emphasis, pattern, movement, unity
  • Spot them and sort them
  • A select-all check
  • Design your own balanced picture in the studio
  • Two short write-ups about composition
  • 1. Learn
  • 2. Sort
  • 3. Select-all
  • 4. Studio
  • 5. Write

🧱 The 6 principles (with how to use each)

PrincipleWhat it meansHow to use it
BalanceVisual weight feels evenDon’t cram everything on one side
ContrastBig differences (light/dark, big/small)Put opposites next to each other to make them pop
EmphasisOne main spot your eye goes first (focal point)Make it brighter, bigger, or more detailed
Pattern / RhythmA shape or colour that repeatsRepeat it to lead the eye along
MovementYour eye travels through the artUse lines and spacing to guide it
UnityEverything looks like it belongs togetherRepeat colours or shapes so it feels whole

🖌️ Studio · Design with a focal point

What to do: Make a small scene with ONE clear focal point. How: (1) place your main object off-centre (rule of thirds), (2) make it the brightest / most detailed thing, (3) repeat one colour somewhere else for unity, (4) add a few lines that point toward it for movement.

Colour Schemes & Mixing 🎨

Now that you can blend any colour, let’s learn which colours look great together. Artists choose a “colour scheme” on purpose to set the mood — and you’ll paint one.

🧭 How this lesson works — read this first

  • Read each coloured box first — it teaches and shows you how.
  • Drop-downs (▾): pick the one correct word.
  • ☑ Select-all boxes: tick every correct one, leave the wrong ones empty.

🎯 Today’s plan

  • 1. Wheel & schemes
  • 2. Warm/cool
  • 3. Select-all
  • 4. Studio
  • 5. Write

🌈 The colour wheel & schemes

SchemeWhat it is
ComplementaryTwo opposite colours (red & green, blue & orange) — high energy
AnalogousColours next to each other (blue, blue-green, green) — calm
MonochromaticONE colour in many tints & shades
TriadicThree colours evenly spaced on the wheel
💡
How to do it: Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) feel hot and lively. Cool colours (blue, green, purple) feel calm. Red & green sit opposite — they are complementary.

🟢 Warm or cool?

Sort the colours.

Red is a colour. Blue is a colour. Orange is . Green is .

🔵 Name the scheme

Match each to its scheme.

Two opposite colours like blue & orange make a scheme. Blue, blue-green and green (neighbours) make an scheme. One blue in light and dark tones is a scheme. Three evenly-spaced colours make a scheme.

🎨 Colours that work together

A colour scheme is a planned set of colours that look good together. Here are the main ones:

SchemeWhat it is
MonochromaticONE colour, plus its lighter tints and darker shades
AnalogousColours that sit NEXT to each other on the wheel (calm, harmonious)
ComplementaryTwo OPPOSITE colours (blue & orange) — bold, high contrast
TriadicTHREE colours evenly spaced on the wheel (red, yellow, blue)
Warm / coolWarm = reds/oranges/yellows; cool = blues/greens/purples
💡
How to do it: For a calm, gentle picture, choose ANALOGOUS colours like blue, blue-green and green. For something that really pops, use COMPLEMENTARY opposites like blue and orange next to each other.

🖐️ Texture & pattern

Texture is how a surface looks or feels — rough, smooth, furry, bumpy. Artists can’t always make you FEEL it, so they make you SEE it with marks.

WordWhat it is
Visual textureTexture you can SEE but not feel (a drawing of bricks)
Actual textureTexture you can really FEEL (real sandpaper, thick paint)
HatchingParallel lines that shade and give texture
Cross-hatchingCrossed lines — darker and rougher
StipplingDots — more dots = darker/rougher
PatternA design that repeats
💡
How to do it: To make an area look rough and dark, add MORE marks — pile up cross-hatching or lots of dots. For a light, smooth look, use just a few soft lines.

⚫⚪ Positive & negative space

Every drawing has two kinds of space, and great artists use BOTH.

WordWhat it is
Positive spaceThe actual object or subject you draw
Negative spaceThe empty area AROUND and between objects

💡
How to do it: Draw a white cup on a dark table: the CUP is the positive space, the dark area around it is the negative space. Filling the negative space with a strong colour makes the cup “pop”. Some clever pictures (like a vase that is also two faces) let the negative space become a second picture!

📦 Two-point perspective

Perspective is how artists make a flat drawing look deep and 3-D. Two-point perspective is perfect for boxes and buildings seen from a corner.

WordWhat it is
Horizon lineThe eye-level line where sky meets ground
Vanishing pointA point on the horizon where parallel lines seem to meet
Two-point perspectiveUses two vanishing points — for a corner view
Vertical edgesStay straight up-and-down (they don’t angle to a point)
Depth (3-D)The illusion that a flat picture has space
💡
How to do it: Draw a box in two-point: mark a horizon line and two vanishing points on it. Draw one vertical line (the front corner). From its top and bottom, draw lines to BOTH vanishing points. The up-and-down edges stay vertical; only the sides shrink toward the points — that’s what makes it look 3-D.

💡

🍎 Still life & observation

A still life is a drawing of objects that do not move — fruit, bottles, books. It is the best way to train your eyes.

WordWhat it is
Still lifeA picture of objects that don’t move (fruit, a vase, books)
ObservationDrawing what you really SEE, not what you imagine
OverlapOne object in front of another — it makes depth
Light sourceWhere the light is coming from
Cast shadowThe shadow an object throws onto the table
💡
How to do it: The golden rule of observation drawing: look at the OBJECT much more than at your paper. Find the big shapes first (a mug is a cylinder), notice what OVERLAPS what, then decide where the LIGHT SOURCE is — the side away from it gets the shading, and the CAST SHADOW falls on the opposite side.

🖨️ Printmaking & repeats

Printmaking means making a picture you can copy again and again — like a stamp. It is how wallpaper, fabric and posters are made.

WordWhat it is

RepeatThe motif printed again and again across the surface

💡
How to do it: Carve or cut a shape, cover it with ink, press it on paper — that’s a PRINT. The small design you repeat is the MOTIF. Print it in a grid and you get a REPEAT pattern (wrapping paper!). Watch out: a stamp prints a MIRROR IMAGE, so letters must be carved backwards to come out the right way round.

🧭 Part 2: Order of Operations (PEMDAS)

  1. Parentheses first
  2. Exponents
  3. Multiply & Divide — left to right
  4. Add & Subtract — left to right
⚠️
Watch out! Multiply and divide are a team — do whichever comes first, left to right. Same for add and subtract.
Worked example

Solve 6 + 2 × (5 − 1)²

  1. Parentheses: 5 − 1 = 4 → 6 + 2 × 4²
  2. Exponent: 4² = 16 → 6 + 2 × 16
  3. Multiply: 2 × 16 = 32 → 6 + 32
  4. Add: 6 + 32 = 38

Solving One- & Two-Step Equations 🔢

An equation is a balance scale. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other — that's how you find the missing number.

🔄 Warm-up · What undoes it?

Every operation has an opposite. Pick the one that undoes each:

To undo + 6 you . To undo × 4 you . To undo − 3 you .

1️⃣ One-Step Equations

Get x alone by doing the inverse operation to both sides.

Example

x + 5 = 12 → subtract 5 from both sides → x = 7.
3x = 21 → divide both sides by 3 → x = 7.

2️⃣ Two-Step Equations

Two-step rule: undo + or − first, then undo × or ÷ (PEMDAS backwards).

Worked example

Solve 2x + 3 = 11

  1. Subtract 3 from both sides → 2x = 8
  2. Divide both sides by 2 → x = 4

Ratios, Rates & Percents 🔢

Ratios compare amounts, rates compare different units, and a percent is just a part out of 100. These show up everywhere — sales, sports, recipes, tips.

🎯 Today's plan

➗ Ratios & Rates

A ratio compares two amounts, like 2 cats to 3 dogs (2:3). Simplify it like a fraction by dividing both sides by the same number: 6:9 = 2:3.

A rate compares different units (miles per hour). A unit rate is "per 1": 120 miles in 2 hours = 60 miles per hour.

💡
To get a unit rate, divide: 120 ÷ 2 = 60 mph. $6 ÷ 3 apples = $2 per apple.

％ Percents

A percent means "out of 100." To find a percent of a number, turn the percent into a decimal and multiply:

Example

25% of 80 → 0.25 × 80 = 20.   10% of 50 → 0.10 × 50 = 5.

🛍️
Discount: a $40 shirt at 25% off → the discount is 25% of 40 = $10, so it costs $30.

📍 Reading Points

A point's address is an ordered pair written (x, y). The x comes first — go across first, then up/down.

Example

To plot (3, 2): start at the origin, go right 3, then up 2. ("Across the hall, then up the stairs.")

🧭

🔢 What an exponent means

In 2³, the big number (2) is the base and the little raised number (3) is the exponent. The exponent tells you how many times to multiply the base by itself.

💡
How to do it: 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2. Multiply left to right: 2 × 2 = 4, then 4 × 2 = 8. So 2³ = 8. (It does NOT mean 2 × 3!)

🟢 Base or exponent?

🎲 What is probability?

Probability is how likely something is to happen. It goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). You write it as a fraction:

🎯
Probability = (ways it CAN happen) ÷ (total possible outcomes).
💡
How to do it: A die has 6 sides. The chance of rolling a 3 is 1 way out of 6 = 1/6. The chance of rolling any number 1–6 is 6/6 = 1 (certain). The chance of rolling a 7 is 0 (impossible).

％ What is a percent?

A percent just means “out of 100.” So 50% = half, 25% = a quarter, and 10% = one tenth. Calculator welcome — but these three are easy by hand:

🎯

💡
How to do it: Find 10% of 80: divide 80 by 10 = 8.   Find 50% of 60: half of 60 = 30.   Find 25% of 40: 40 ÷ 4 = 10.   A $50 jacket with 10% off: 10% of 50 = $5 off, so you pay $45.

📐 Area & perimeter

🎯
Perimeter = the distance ALL THE WAY AROUND (add up every side).   Area = the space INSIDE (for a rectangle: length × width), measured in square units.
💡
How to do it: A rectangle 5 across and 3 up: perimeter = 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16. Area = 5 × 3 = 15 square units. Tip: a square has 4 equal sides, so perimeter = side × 4.

🔢 Rounding & estimation

Rounding makes a number simpler by bumping it to the nearest 10 or 100. Estimating uses rounding to get a quick, close answer.

🎯
The rule: look at the next digit. 5 or more → round up. 4 or less → stay the same.
💡
How to do it: Round 47 to the nearest 10: the ones digit is 7 (5 or more) → round up to 50. Round 42: the ones digit is 2 (4 or less) → stays at 40. To estimate 19 + 22, round to 20 + 20 = about 40.

🔢 Number patterns & sequences

A sequence is a list of numbers that follows a rule. Spot the rule and you can find the next number!

🎯
Look at the gap between the numbers. Same gap each time? The rule is “add” (or “subtract”) that amount.
💡
How to do it: 2, 4, 6, 8, … The gap is +2 each time, so the next number is 10.  20, 18, 16, … the gap is −2, so the next is 14.  5, 10, 15, … the rule is “add 5”, so next is 20.

✖️➗ Multiplication & division

Two everyday skills that go together like a team.

🎯
Multiplication is fast adding of equal groups: 3 × 4 means “four, three times” = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.  Division shares into equal groups: 12 ÷ 3 = 4. They are opposites!
💡
How to do it: 3 × 4 = 12, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3 — that’s a “fact family”. Tip for multiplying: skip-count. For 5 × 3, count 5, 10, 15. Calculator always welcome.

🍕 Understanding fractions

A fraction is a part of a whole. Think of a pizza cut into equal slices!

🎯
A fraction has two numbers. The bottom (denominator) tells how many EQUAL parts in total. The top (numerator) tells how many you HAVE. So 1/4 = 1 part out of 4.
💡
How to do it: Cut a pizza into 4 equal slices and take 1: you have 1/4. Take 3 slices: 3/4. Cut into 2 and take 1: 1/2 (a half). The bigger the bottom number, the SMALLER each slice (1/8 is smaller than 1/2).

📊 Reading graphs & data

A graph turns numbers into a picture so you can SEE the answer quickly.

WordWhat it is

💡
How to do it: Say a bar graph shows favourite pets: Dogs 8, Cats 5, Fish 2. The TALLEST bar (Dogs, 8) is the MOST popular; the SHORTEST (Fish, 2) is the least. To find “how many more dogs than cats?” you SUBTRACT: 8 − 5 = 3.

🔢 Factors, multiples, odd & even

Three handy number ideas that make times tables click.

WordWhat it means
Even numberDivides by 2 with nothing left over — ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
Odd numberDoes NOT divide by 2 evenly — ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
FactorA number that divides EXACTLY into another (factors of 6: 1, 2, 3, 6)
MultipleThe answer when you times a number (multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20)
💡
How to do it: FACTORS go INTO a number; MULTIPLES come OUT of it. Factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 (they all divide in exactly). Multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36… (12 times something). And the quick odd/even test: just look at the LAST digit.

📝 Cracking word problems

Word problems feel scary — until you use a plan. Here is a 4-step method that works every time.

StepWhat to do
1. ReadRead it twice. What is the question actually asking?
2. Find the numbersUnderline the numbers and what they mean
3. Choose the operationAdd, subtract, multiply or divide?
4. Solve & checkWork it out, then ask “does this make sense?”
💡
How to do it: Clue words tell you the operation: “in total / altogether” → ADD. “how many more / left / fewer” → SUBTRACT. “each / groups of” → MULTIPLY. “shared equally / split” → DIVIDE. Example: “Ella has 12 stickers and shares them equally between 3 friends.” Shared equally → DIVIDE → 12 ÷ 3 = 4 each.

🟨 Multiply or divide?

Parts of Speech & Strong Sentences 📖

Words have jobs. Know each word's job and you can build clear sentences and fix mistakes.

🧩 The 8 Parts of Speech

PartIts jobExamples
NounNames a person, place, thing, or ideaartist, studio, courage
PronounReplaces a nounshe, it, they, we
VerbShows action or beingpaint, run, is, became
AdjectiveDescribes a nounbright, three, curious
AdverbDescribes a verb/adjective/adverb (often -ly)quickly, very, often
PrepositionShows position or relationshipunder, before, with
ConjunctionJoins words or ideasand, but, because
InterjectionShows sudden emotionWow! Oh no! Yes!
🎨
Art connection: "The curious (adj) artist boldly (adv) painted (verb) a mural (noun)."

🏗️ Building a Complete Sentence

Subject + Predicate

Subject = who/what it's about. Predicate = what they do or are (has the verb).

"My older sister paints every weekend."

ProblemWhat it isFix
FragmentMissing a subject or verb. "Because she loves art.""She joined the club because she loves art."
Run-onTwo sentences jammed together."She paints, and she also sketches."

Practice — pick the correct sentence

1Which is a complete sentence?
2Which fixes the run-on "I love art I draw daily"?

📚 Read & Answer

Maya had always loved color, but she had never tried painting a mural. When her art teacher asked for volunteers to decorate the school's empty hallway, Maya's hand shot up before she could second-guess herself. For two weeks she sketched, mixed paints, and climbed ladders after school.

The morning the mural was revealed, students stopped and stared. A giant sunrise spread across the wall in warm oranges, balanced by a cool blue sky. Maya felt nervous and proud at the same time. She realized that the scariest projects often became the ones she was most glad she tried.

1What is the passage mainly about?
2Raising her hand quickly shows Maya is…
3Which best states the theme?

Good writers don't always say things straight. They use word-tricks that paint pictures and stir feelings. Learn to spot — and use — them.

🔤 Warm-up · Name that trick

"The stars danced in the sky" → . "She is as brave as a lion" → . "I've told you a million times" → .

🎭 The Types of Figurative Language

TypeWhat it doesExample
SimileCompares two things using like or as"as busy as a bee"
MetaphorSays one thing is another (no like/as)"Time is a thief"
PersonificationGives human traits to non-human things"The wind whispered"
HyperboleHuge exaggeration for effect"I could eat a horse"
IdiomA phrase that doesn't mean its literal words"break a leg" (= good luck)
OnomatopoeiaA word that imitates a soundbuzz, splash, pop
AlliterationSame beginning sound, repeated"wild and windy"
💡
Simile vs. metaphor: a simile uses like or as ("brave as a lion"); a metaphor says it is ("she is a lion").

📚 Spot It in Text

The old car coughed and groaned as it struggled up the hill. The morning sun was a warm blanket across Maya's shoulders, and the leaves whispered secrets in the breeze. "I'm so hungry I could eat this whole town," she laughed, hopping out as the door went creak.

Reading Strategies 📖

Good readers do more than sound out words — they find the main idea, read between the lines, and use clues to figure out new words.

🎯 Today's plan

  • Find the main idea vs. the supporting details
  • Make an inference (read between the lines)

🔤 Warm-up · Context clue

"The desert was so arid that not a single plant could survive." The word arid probably means .

🎯 Main Idea vs. Details

The main idea is what a paragraph is mostly about. Details are the smaller facts and examples that support it.

💡
Ask: "What is this mostly about?" The answer that covers the whole paragraph (not just one sentence) is the main idea.

🔎 Inference & Context Clues

An inference is a smart guess using clues + what you already know — the author doesn't say it directly. Context clues are nearby words that hint at a new word's meaning.

Inference

"Mia grabbed her umbrella and pulled on her boots." You can infer it's probably raining — even though it never says so.

📚 Read & Answer

Sea otters do something clever at dinnertime. Floating on their backs, they balance a flat rock on their bellies and smash shellfish against it to crack them open. Pups learn this trick by watching their mothers for hours. Scientists were amazed to discover that some otters even keep a favorite rock, tucking it into a pouch of loose skin under their arm so they never lose it.

1What is the main idea?
2From the passage you can infer that otters are…
3Using context, a "pouch" is most like a…

Prefixes, Suffixes & Roots 📖

Crack open a long word and you can often figure out its meaning from its parts — a beginning, a middle, and an end.

🔤 Warm-up · What does it mean?

"un-" means , "re-" means , "-less" means .

🧩 The Word Parts

PartWhereExamples
PrefixAt the start — changes the meaningun- (not), re- (again), pre- (before), dis- (not)
RootThe base — the core meaning"play" in replaying, "joy" in joyful
SuffixAt the end — often changes the job/type-ful (full of), -less (without), -ed, -ing
💡
unhappy = un (not) + happy → "not happy". Break a word into parts and the meaning appears!

Punctuation & Grammar Power 📖

Punctuation is how your writing “talks” — it tells the reader when to pause, what belongs together, and who owns what. Today you fix a lot of sentences and then write your own, carefully punctuated.

🎯 Today’s plan (a full 45 minutes)

✏️ Comma rules

  • Lists: I bought apples, bread, and milk.
  • After an intro: After the game, we ate.
  • Joining two full sentences with and/but/so: I ran, but I missed the bus.
💡
An apostrophe shows ownership (the dog’s bone) OR a contraction (do not → don’t). It is never used to make a word plural.

🔴 Run-on or fragment?

Label each one.

“She runs every morning she loves it.” is a . “Because it was raining.” is a . The run-on is best fixed by adding a .

Reading Deeper: Main Idea, Theme & Inference 📖

Good readers don’t just see the words — they figure out the point, the message, and the things the writer hints at without saying. Today you read a real short story and dig in.

🎯 Today’s plan (about 45 minutes)

  • Main idea vs. little details
  • Theme — the lesson or message
  • Inference — reading between the lines
  • Read a story, answer questions, and write your own response
  • 1. Main idea
  • 2. Theme
  • 3. Inference
  • 4. Read
  • 5. Write

🔑 The three skills

SkillWhat it means
Main ideaWhat the whole thing is mostly about (the big point)
DetailA small fact that supports the main idea
ThemeThe deeper life lesson or message (e.g., “never give up”)
InferenceA smart guess using clues + what you already know
💡
An inference is “clues + your brain.” The story never says Maya is proud — but she taped the slip to the fridge, so you can infer she is.

Read this short story:

Maya had failed her driving-permit test twice. The third morning, her little brother found her at the kitchen table, surrounded by flash cards, eyes tired. “Why don’t you just quit?” he asked. Maya didn’t look up. “Because quitting is the only way to actually fail,” she said. That afternoon she walked out of the testing center holding a small paper slip, and she didn’t say a word — she just taped it to the fridge where everyone could see the word PASSED. Her brother grinned. The flash cards stayed on the table for a week, like a trophy.

🟢 Did you get it?

Answer from the story you just read.

The main idea of the story is mostly about . We can infer Maya felt at the end because she . The detail that she failed “twice” before supports the theme of .

🔵 Main idea or detail?

Label each statement.

“Maya passed her driving test after failing twice.” is the . “Her brother found her at the kitchen table.” is a . A theme you could write for this story is .

🟡 Context clues

Use the sentence to guess the word’s meaning.

“The flash cards stayed on the table like a trophy.” Here, “trophy” suggests the cards were a sign of . From “eyes tired… surrounded by flash cards,” we can tell Maya had been .

Writing a Strong Paragraph 📖

A good paragraph isn’t random sentences — it’s built in a clear order, like a burger. Today you learn the parts, then actually build two solid paragraphs of your own.

🧭 How this lesson works — read this first

This is a big one, so here’s the plan. Do the sections in order, top to bottom:

  • Read each coloured box first — it teaches and shows you how.
  • Drop-downs (▾): pick the one correct word.
  • ☑ Select-all boxes: tick every correct one, leave the wrong ones empty.
  • Type-in boxes: work it out (scratch paper / calculator is fine) and type the answer.
  • Press the Check buttons to see green (right) and red (wrong).
📊
Watch the bar at the very top — it fills as you finish. Keep going until it says “Lesson complete!” That’s how you know you really did the whole thing.

🎯 Today’s plan

  • The 4 parts of a strong paragraph
  • Spot the parts and sort them
  • A select-all check on good writing
  • Build two full paragraphs of your own
  • 1. Parts
  • 2. Sort
  • 3. Select-all
  • 4. Write 1
  • 5. Write 2

🍔 The “burger” paragraph (how to build one)

PartIts job
1. Topic sentence (top bun)States your main point — what the paragraph is about
2. Evidence / details (patty)Facts, reasons, or examples that back it up
3. Explanation (cheese)You explain HOW the evidence proves your point
4. Closing sentence (bottom bun)Wraps it up or restates the point in a fresh way
💡
How to do it: Topic: “Dogs make great first pets.” → Evidence: “They’re loyal and easy to train.” → Explanation: “Because they learn commands fast, a kid can care for one successfully.” → Closing: “For a responsible kid, a dog is a perfect starter pet.”
🔗
Transitions glue sentences together: for example, also, however, because, as a result, finally.

🟢 Name that part

Use the burger model.

The sentence that states your main point is the . Facts and examples that back it up are the . Words like “for example” and “however” are . The sentence that wraps it all up is the .

🔍 Using context clues

When you hit a word you don’t know, you don’t need a dictionary — the surrounding words usually give it away. That’s using context clues.

Clue typeHow it helps
DefinitionThe sentence explains the word right there
SynonymA nearby word means the same thing
AntonymA nearby word means the opposite (look for “but”, “unlike”)
ExampleExamples nearby show what it means
💡
How to do it: “The arid desert had no water for miles.” You don’t know “arid”? The clue “no water” tells you it means dry. That’s a definition/example clue.

🟢 Use the clue

Guess the bold word from the sentence.

“She was elated — she jumped for joy.” Elated means . “The food was bland, with no flavour at all.” Bland means . “Unlike his timid sister, Max was bold.” Timid means . “The vast, huge ocean stretched on forever.” Vast means .

What kind of clue is it?

“A foal, which is a baby horse, ran in the field.” → . “He was furious, unlike his calm brother.” → . “She felt joyful and happy all day.” → . “Citrus fruits, like oranges and lemons, are sour.” → .

Figurative Language: Similes, Metaphors & More 📖

Writers make words come alive by NOT saying exactly what they mean. Today you master the six big tools of figurative language — and use them yourself.

🧭 How this lesson works — read this first

  • Read each coloured box first — it teaches and shows you how.
  • Drop-downs (▾): pick the one correct word.
  • ☑ Select-all boxes: tick every correct one, leave the wrong ones empty.

  • 2. Name it

🗣️ Figurative language — saying more than the plain words

Figurative language means words used in a colourful, not-literal way to paint pictures and feelings.

ToolWhat it is
SimileCompares two things using “like” or “as” — brave as a lion
MetaphorSays one thing IS another — the classroom was a zoo
PersonificationGives human actions to non-human things — the wind whispered
HyperboleA huge exaggeration — I’ve told you a million times
OnomatopoeiaA word that sounds like its noise — buzz, splash, bang
IdiomA saying that doesn’t mean it literally — it’s raining cats and dogs
💡
How to do it: “The stars danced in the sky” is PERSONIFICATION (stars can’t really dance). “Her bag weighed a ton” is HYPERBOLE (a big exaggeration). “The bees buzzed” uses ONOMATOPOEIA (buzz sounds like the noise).

🟢 Name the tool

Read each example and choose.

“As quiet as a mouse” is a . “Time is a thief” is a . “The flowers nodded their heads” is . “I could eat a horse” is .

🏷️ Nouns & pronouns

Two building blocks of every sentence — the naming words and their handy stand-ins.

WordWhat it is
NounA person, place or thing (girl, city, ball)
Common nounA general name — dog, city, girl (lowercase)
Proper nounA specific name — Rex, Paris, Emma (always CAPITAL)
PronounA word that replaces a noun: he, she, it, they, we
Plural nounMore than one — usually add -s (dog → dogs)
💡
How to do it: “Emma lost Emma’s book” sounds clunky. Swap in a PRONOUN: “Emma lost her book.” Pronouns stop you repeating the same noun. And remember: PROPER nouns (Emma, Paris) always start with a CAPITAL letter; common nouns (girl, city) do not.

🗣️ Idioms & everyday expressions

An idiom is a phrase that means something different from the actual words. English is full of them!

“Under the weather”Feeling ill
“Hit the books”Start studying
LiteralThe plain, word-for-word meaning
💡
How to do it: Idioms are NOT literal. Nobody expects actual cats to fall from the sky — “raining cats and dogs” just means heavy rain. When you meet a strange phrase, ask: does this make sense word-for-word? If not, it is probably an idiom, and the words around it will hint at the real meaning.

📕 Dictionary & glossary skills

WordWhat it is
DictionaryA book (or app) listing words and their meanings
Alphabetical orderA to Z order — how the words are arranged
Guide wordsThe first and last word on a page, shown at the top
EntryOne word plus its meaning(s)

💡
How to do it: Finding a word fast: dictionaries are in ALPHABETICAL ORDER, so compare the FIRST letter — if they match, compare the second, and so on (cat comes before cup because a < u). The Scientific Method & Lab Safety 🔬

Science is a method for figuring out how the world works. Learn the steps scientists use.

🎯 Today's plan

A student tests: "Does the amount of water change how tall a sunflower grows?"

Amount of water (changed) →
Height of the sunflower (measured) →
Same pot, soil, sunlight for every plant →

New to you? You'll learn it right below. 👇

🔁 The Scientific Method

  1. Question — What are you curious about?
  2. Research — Find out what's already known.
  3. Hypothesis — A testable "If… then…" prediction.
  4. Experiment — Test it, changing only one thing.
  5. Analyze — Collect data, look for patterns.
  6. Conclusion — Was your hypothesis supported?
💡
A good hypothesis is testable. "If I play music for my plant, then it will grow taller than one with no music."

🎚️ Variables: the heart of a fair test

VariableMeaningPlant example
IndependentThe ONE thing you changeWhether music plays
DependentWhat you measureHow tall the plant grows
ControlledWhat you keep the sameWater, sunlight, soil, pot
🎯
Tip: I change the Independent variable. The Dependent variable Depends on it.

Practice — label the variables

🧪 Lab Safety Rules

  • Wear safety goggles when told to
  • Never eat or drink in the lab
  • Tie back long hair and roll up loose sleeves
  • Tell your teacher about any spill right away
  • Know where the sink, fire extinguisher, and exit are
  • Never mix chemicals unless instructed
⚠️
Golden rule: when in doubt, ask the teacher before you act.

Matter: States & Changes 🔬

Everything around you is matter — anything that has mass and takes up space. Today: the states of matter and how matter changes.

🎯 Today's plan

  • The three main states of matter and their particles
  • Changes of state (melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation)
  • Physical vs. chemical changes
  • Signs that a new substance formed
  • 1. Warm-up
  • 2. States of matter
  • 3. Physical vs chemical
  • 4. Practice & data
  • 5. Quick check

🧊 Warm-up · Solid, liquid, or gas?

An ice cube is a , orange juice is a , and the steam over a hot drink is a .

🧊💧☁️ The States of Matter

StateShape & volumeWhat the particles do
SolidKeeps its shape and volumePacked tight, only vibrate in place
LiquidTakes the container's shape, keeps its volumeSlide past each other
GasFills the whole container, no fixed shape or volumeFly around fast and far apart

Changes of state (adding or removing heat)

  • Melting: solid → liquid (ice → water)
  • Freezing: liquid → solid (water → ice)
  • Evaporation / boiling: liquid → gas (water → steam)
  • Condensation: gas → liquid (steam → droplets on a mirror)
💡
Add heat → particles move faster and spread out (solid→liquid→gas). Remove heat → they slow down and pack together (gas→liquid→solid).

⚗️ Physical vs. Chemical Changes

Physical changeChemical change
What happensLooks different, but it's the same substanceA brand-new substance forms
ExamplesMelting, cutting, tearing, dissolving, bendingBurning, rusting, baking, rotting, fizzing tablets
Reversible?Often yesUsually no
🔎
Signs of a chemical change: a new color, bubbles/gas, heat or light given off, a new smell, or something that can't easily change back.

Energy: Forms & Changes 🔬

Energy is the ability to make something happen — to move, heat, light up, or grow. It comes in many forms and is always changing from one to another.

🎯 Today's plan

  • Kinetic (moving) vs. potential (stored) energy
  • The main forms of energy

⚡ Warm-up · Moving or stored?

A ball rolling downhill → , a book resting on a high shelf → , a running cheetah → , a stretched rubber band → .

🏃 Kinetic vs. Potential

TypeWhat it isExample
KineticThe energy of motionA rolling ball, wind, a running dog
PotentialStored energy, ready to be usedA ball at the top of a hill, a stretched spring
🎢
At the top of a roller-coaster hill you have lots of potential energy; as you race down it turns into kinetic energy.

🔆 Forms of Energy

FormWhere you see it
LightThe sun, a lamp
Thermal (heat)A warm cup of cocoa, a fire
SoundA vibrating guitar string
ElectricalElectricity in a wire
ChemicalStored in food and batteries
MechanicalMoving machines and objects
💡
Big rule: energy is never created or destroyed — it just changes form. A battery's chemical energy → electrical → light + heat in a flashlight.

FrictionSlows things down when surfaces rub; gives grip

💡

🧬 Heredity & genetics

Heredity is how traits pass from parents to children. Inside your cells, DNA carries the instructions, packed into genes. You get one copy of each gene from each parent.

WordMeaning
TraitA feature like eye colour or height
GeneA piece of DNA with instructions for a trait
DominantThe “stronger” version — shows up if present (BIG letter, B)
RecessiveThe “quieter” version — only shows if there’s no dominant (small letter, b)
💡
How to do it: A Punnett square crosses two parents. If both are Bb (brown eyes, carrying blue): the children can be BB, Bb, Bb, bb. Three show brown (have a B), one shows blue (bb). So 3 out of 4 brown.

The Water Cycle: Earth’s Endless Loop 💧

💧 The water cycle

Earth’s water is used over and over in a loop powered by the Sun. The same water can be in a cloud today and in your glass next week.

StepWhat happens
EvaporationThe Sun heats water so it turns into invisible water vapour (gas) and rises
CondensationVapour cools high up and turns back into tiny droplets, forming clouds
PrecipitationDroplets join, get heavy and fall as rain, snow, sleet or hail
CollectionWater gathers in oceans, lakes and rivers — and the loop starts again
💡
How to do it: Order of the loop: EVAPORATION (up as vapour) → CONDENSATION (clouds form) → PRECIPITATION (rain falls) → COLLECTION (water gathers) → and back to evaporation. The Sun’s heat drives the whole thing.

🐾 Animal groups

GroupKey features

🪨 Rocks & minerals

The ground beneath you is made of rock. Geologists sort rocks into three types by how they formed.

TypeHow it forms · example
IgneousFrom cooled melted rock (lava/magma) — granite, obsidian
SedimentaryFrom layers of sand and mud pressed together — sandstone, limestone
MetamorphicChanged by great heat and pressure — marble, slate
MineralA natural solid that rocks are made of — quartz, gold
Rock cycleRocks slowly change from one type into another, over and over
💡
How to do it: Clues to remember: IGNEOUS = “ignite” → made by FIRE/heat cooling down (lava). SEDIMENTARY = “sediment” → made of LAYERS pressed together. METAMORPHIC = “metamorphosis” → CHANGED by heat and pressure. And the ROCK CYCLE means any rock can eventually become another type.

Earth’s resources are the things we use from nature. Some can run out — so we look after them.

WordWhat it means
Natural resourceSomething useful from nature — water, wood, coal, sunlight

🌙 The Moon & its phases

The Moon is Earth’s only natural satellite. It seems to change shape through the month — but it never really does!

WordWhat it is
MoonA rocky body that orbits Earth
OrbitThe Moon’s path around Earth (about a month)
PhaseThe shape of the lit part of the Moon we can see
New moonWe see almost none of it lit
Full moonWe see the whole lit circle
CrescentJust a thin curved sliver is lit
💡
How to do it: Key idea: the Moon makes NO light of its own — it REFLECTS sunlight. As it ORBITS Earth (about a month), we see different amounts of its lit half. That’s a PHASE. NEW MOON = we see almost nothing lit; FULL MOON = we see the whole circle; a CRESCENT is the thin sliver in between. The Moon isn’t changing shape — our view of it is.

The Human Body & Its Systems 🫀

Your body is a team of systems working together every second. Meet the main ones and what each does.

🎯 Today's plan

🤔 Warm-up · Find these on yourself

Point to (or picture) each of these on your own body:

  • Your heart — slightly left of center in your chest
  • Your lungs — they fill your chest when you breathe in
  • Your brain — inside your skull
  • Your biggest muscle — the gluteus (your seat!)
  • Feel your pulse at your wrist or neck — that's your heart pumping blood

🧬 How the Body Is Built

Your body is organized from the tiniest pieces all the way up to the whole you:

  1. Cells — the smallest living building blocks (you have trillions!)
  2. Tissues — groups of similar cells working together (like muscle tissue)
  3. Organs — different tissues teamed up for a job (like the heart)
  4. Organ systems — organs working together (like the circulatory system)
  5. Organism — all the systems together = the whole body (you!)
💡
Smallest → biggest: Cells → Tissues → Organs → Systems → Organism.

🫀 The Major Body Systems

SystemMain jobKey parts
SkeletalSupports the body, protects organs, makes blood cellsBones, joints (206 bones!)
MuscularMoves the body, holds posture, makes heatMuscles, tendons
CirculatoryPumps blood to carry oxygen & nutrients everywhereHeart, blood, blood vessels
RespiratoryTakes in oxygen, gets rid of carbon dioxideLungs, trachea, diaphragm
DigestiveBreaks down food into energy & nutrientsStomach, intestines, liver
NervousControls the body and senses the worldBrain, spinal cord, nerves
ExcretoryRemoves liquid waste from the bloodKidneys, bladder
🤝
Teamwork: When you run, the respiratory system grabs oxygen, the circulatory system delivers it, the muscular system moves you, and the nervous system controls it all — at the same time!

Circulation & Breathing 🫀

Two systems team up to keep every cell alive: the circulatory system (heart + blood) and the respiratory system (lungs + breathing).

🎯 Today's plan

  • How the heart and blood vessels move blood
  • How the lungs trade oxygen for carbon dioxide
  • How the two systems work together

💓 Warm-up · Measure your own body

Do these now — you're about to study exactly what they measure:

  • Put two fingers on your wrist or neck and find your pulse
  • Count the beats for 15 seconds, then multiply by 4 — that's your heart rate (beats per minute)
  • Now count how many breaths you take in 30 seconds
  • Do 15 jumping jacks, then check your pulse again — faster, right? Why? (You'll find out below.)

🫀 The Heart & Blood

Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. It pumps blood every second of your life — roughly 60–100 beats a minute at rest.

VesselIts job
ArteriesCarry blood away from the heart (oxygen-rich)
VeinsCarry blood back to the heart
CapillariesTiny vessels where blood trades oxygen & nutrients with cells
💡
Memory tip: Arteries carry blood Away. Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to cells and hauls away waste like carbon dioxide.

🫁 The Lungs & Gas Exchange

When you breathe in, air travels down your trachea into your lungs, all the way to millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli.

  1. You breathe in oxygen from the air.
  2. In the alveoli, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
  3. You breathe out carbon dioxide, the waste gas.
  4. The diaphragm (a muscle under your lungs) pulls down to help you inhale.
🤝
That's why exercise makes you breathe harder: your muscles need more oxygen, so your heart beats faster and your lungs work harder to keep up.

Digestion: From Food to Fuel 🍎

Every bite you eat goes on a journey of about 9 metres through your body, getting broken down so your cells can use it for energy.

🍽️ Warm-up · Think it through

  • Picture the food going down a tube to your stomach

🛤️ The Journey of Food

  1. Mouth — teeth chew; saliva starts breaking food down.
  2. Esophagus — a muscular tube squeezes food down to the stomach.
  3. Stomach — churns food and mixes it with acid into a mush.
  4. Small intestine — nutrients pass into the blood here.
  5. Large intestine — soaks up water; what's left becomes waste.
💡
Most of the real absorption of nutrients happens in the small intestine — it's long and lined with tiny folds to grab every bit.

The nervous system is made of the brain, the spinal cord, and a body-wide network of nerves.

  1. Your senses pick up information (light, sound, smell, taste, touch).
  2. Nerves carry that as electrical signals to the brain.
  3. The brain makes sense of it and decides what to do.
  4. The brain sends signals back through nerves to move your muscles.

This happens in a flash — a nerve signal can travel faster than 100 metres per second!

🔵 Joints

A joint is where two bones meet.

Your knee and elbow bend one way like a door — those are . Your shoulder and hip can swing in circles — those are . The bones in your skull are locked together and don’t move — those are . Tough bands called connect muscle to bone.

🟡 Muscle pairs

Muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs.

To bend your elbow, the on the front shortens (pulls). To straighten it again, the on the back pulls the other way. Because one pulls while the other relaxes, we call them an . Muscles attached to bones that you control are called .

📚 Why Geography Matters

Long before phones could show a blue dot on a map, explorers crossed oceans using only the stars, a compass, and lines of latitude and longitude. Knowing exactly where you are has always shaped human history — where cities grew, which countries traded, and how armies moved.

Geography still shapes daily life. Mountains and rivers decide where roads and farms can go. A country near the Equator has a very different climate from one near the poles. When you understand maps, news about faraway places makes a lot more sense.

Social Studies · Lesson 2

The 3 Branches of Government 🏛️

The U.S. Constitution splits the government into three branches so no single person or group gets too much power. Here's how it works.

🎯 Today's plan

  • The 3 branches and what each one does
  • How checks and balances keep power even
  • How a bill becomes a law
  • What a veto is
  • 1. Warm-up
  • 2. Three branches
  • 3. Checks & balances
  • 4. How a bill becomes law
  • 5. Quick check

🏛️ Warm-up · Who does what?

The branch that makes laws → , the branch that carries out laws → , the branch that interprets laws → .

⚖️ The Three Branches

BranchWho's in itWhat it does
LegislativeCongress = the Senate + the House of RepresentativesMakes the laws
ExecutiveThe President + Vice President + CabinetCarries out (enforces) the laws
JudicialThe Supreme Court + other federal courtsInterprets the laws — decides what they mean and if they're constitutional
💡
Quick way to remember: Legislative = Legislate (make). Executive = Execute (do). Judicial = Judge (decide).

🔄 Checks & Balances

Each branch can limit the others, so no branch becomes too powerful:

  • The President can veto (reject) a bill from Congress.
  • Congress can override a veto with a 2/3 vote — and can impeach officials.
  • The Courts can declare a law unconstitutional and cancel it.
  • Congress approves the judges the President picks.
⚖️
This back-and-forth is called checks and balances — the heart of how the Constitution shares power.

📜 How a Bill Becomes a Law

  1. An idea is written up as a bill.
  2. It's introduced in Congress (the House or the Senate).
  3. A committee studies, debates, and may change it.
  4. Both the House and the Senate vote — it must pass both.
  5. It goes to the President.
  6. The President signs it → it becomes a law. (Or vetoes it.)
  7. If vetoed, Congress can still pass it with a 2/3 override vote.

The Constitution & Bill of Rights 🗽

The Constitution is the rulebook for the whole U.S. government. Its first ten amendments — the Bill of Rights — protect the freedoms of every person.

🎯 Today's plan

🗽 Warm-up · Which freedom?

Sharing your opinion about the government → freedom of , going to any church, mosque, or temple → freedom of , a newspaper printing the news → freedom of the .

📜 The Constitution

The Constitution is the plan and rulebook for the U.S. government — it sets up the three branches and the laws they must follow. It was written in 1787 and is still the highest law in the country.

An amendment is an official change or addition to the Constitution. There are 27 of them so far.

💡
The Constitution can be changed — but on purpose it's hard to do, so rights stay protected over time.

🗽 The Bill of Rights

The Bill of Rights is the name for the first 10 amendments. They protect the freedoms of the people. The famous 1st Amendment protects five freedoms:

  • Freedom of speech
  • Freedom of religion
  • Freedom of the press
  • Freedom of assembly (gathering peacefully)
  • The right to petition (ask the government to fix things)

The American Revolution 🇺🇸

How did 13 colonies break away from the most powerful empire on Earth? Today you read the story, learn the key people and events, and put the timeline in order.

🎯 Today’s plan (a full 45 minutes)

  • Causes — why the colonists were angry
  • Key events — from the Tea Party to Yorktown

📜 The short story

In the 1760s and 1770s, Britain taxed its American colonies to pay for war debts — on things like tea, paper, and stamps. The colonists had no representatives in the British Parliament, so they protested: “No taxation without representation!”

Anger boiled over at the Boston Tea Party (1773), when colonists dumped British tea into the harbor. Fighting began at Lexington and Concord (1775). On July 4, 1776, the colonies approved the Declaration of Independence, mostly written by Thomas Jefferson. George Washington led the Continental Army, and after years of war the Americans won the final battle at Yorktown (1781).

The Civil War: A Nation Divided 🔵🔴

Heroes who fought for freedom included Frederick Douglass (a formerly enslaved writer and speaker) and Harriet Tubman (who guided enslaved people to freedom on the Underground Railroad).

Read this:

By 1861 the United States had split in two. The Northern states (the Union) and the Southern states (the Confederacy) disagreed bitterly — most of all about slavery, which the Southern economy depended on. When Abraham Lincoln became president, eleven Southern states left the country. The war began when the South attacked Fort Sumter. For four long years brother sometimes fought brother. In 1863 Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation declared enslaved people in the rebelling states to be free. The Union finally won in 1865 at Appomattox, the country stayed together, and slavery was ended for good by the 13th Amendment.

Ending slavery was only the beginning. This lesson follows what happened next — the new amendments, the unfair laws that pushed back, and the brave people who fought for equal rights.

📜 The three Reconstruction Amendments

AmendmentWhat it did
13thEnded slavery everywhere in the U.S.
14thMade formerly enslaved people citizens with equal protection
15thSaid the right to vote can’t be denied because of race
💡
How to do it: A memory trick: 13 = free, 14 = citizen, 15 = vote. They go in order: first you’re free, then a citizen, then you can vote.

Read this:

When the Civil War ended in 1865, the country had to rebuild — a time called Reconstruction. Three new amendments were added: the 13th ended slavery, the 14th made formerly enslaved people citizens with equal protection under the law, and the 15th said the right to vote couldn’t be denied because of race. But progress didn’t last. Southern states passed Jim Crow laws that segregated (separated) Black and white people and blocked Black citizens from voting. Nearly a century later, the Civil Rights Movement fought back. Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in 1955. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. led peaceful marches and gave his “I Have a Dream” speech in 1963. In 1964 the Civil Rights Act finally outlawed segregation.

How to do it: Think cause → effect: the 1929 crash → banks failed → people lost jobs & homes (the Depression). FDR’s response → the New Deal → government jobs and Social Security.

Read this:

In October 1929, the stock market crashed — fortunes vanished overnight, banks failed, and the country fell into the Great Depression, the worst economic slump in U.S. history. About one in four workers lost their jobs. Families lost their homes and savings. On top of it, a terrible drought turned farmland into a giant dust storm called the Dust Bowl, forcing farmers to flee. In 1933, President Franklin D. Roosevelt (FDR) launched the New Deal — government programs that created jobs (building roads, parks, and dams), helped the needy, and added protections like Social Security. Recovery was slow, but the New Deal gave people hope and jobs.

The Cold War 🌍

After World War II, two giant countries stared each other down for over forty years — without ever fighting directly. Today you learn what the Cold War was, and how the world competed instead of clashing.

🧭 How this lesson works — read this first

  • Read each coloured box first — it teaches and shows you how.
  • Drop-downs (▾): pick the one correct word.
  • ☑ Select-all boxes: tick every correct one, leave the wrong ones empty.

  • 2. Read

🌍 A war without direct fighting

TermWhat it was
Cold WarA tense rivalry with no direct “hot” fighting between the two sides
United StatesLed the capitalist, democratic side
Soviet Union (USSR)Led the communist side
Arms raceCompeting to build more powerful weapons
Space RaceCompeting to reach space and the Moon
Berlin WallA wall dividing Berlin; its fall (1989) signalled the war’s end
💡
How to do it: Remember: the Cold War was “cold” because the U.S. and USSR never fought each other head-on. They competed instead — building weapons (arms race) and racing to space. It ended around 1989–1991.

Read this:

After World War II, the world’s two strongest countries — the United States and the Soviet Union (USSR) — became rivals. This long standoff (about 1947–1991) was called the Cold War because the two sides never fought each other directly in a big “hot” war. Instead they competed in other ways. The U.S. believed in capitalism and democracy; the Soviet Union believed in communism. They raced to build weapons (the arms race) and to reach space (the Space Race). A divided city, Berlin, was split by a wall; when the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, the Cold War was ending. The USSR broke apart in 1991.

Each branch can limit the others — a system called checks and balances.

💡
How to do it: The feudal ladder from top to bottom: KING → NOBLES/LORDS → KNIGHTS → PEASANTS. Lords built CASTLES for defence, knights wore armour and protected the lord, and peasants did the farming. Remember: Middle Ages = knights, castles and kingdoms.

Read this:

The Middle Ages (or medieval times) was the long period in Europe after ancient Rome fell — about a thousand years. Society was organised by feudalism: a king gave land to powerful nobles (lords), who were protected by armoured soldiers called knights. At the bottom, most people were peasants who farmed the land. To stay safe from attacks, lords built strong stone castles with high walls. It was a world of kingdoms, knights, and castles.

These voyages connected faraway continents — but they also brought great hardship to the native peoples who already lived there.

🗺️ Reading a map

WordWhat it is
Compass roseShows north, south, east and west on a map
Key / legendExplains what the map’s symbols mean
ScaleShows how map distance compares to real distance
LandformA natural feature of the land (mountain, valley, island)
IslandLand with water all the way around it
PeninsulaLand with water on three sides
💡
How to do it: Remember the map tools: COMPASS ROSE = which way (N, S, E, W). KEY = what the symbols mean. SCALE = how far. And landforms: an ISLAND has water ALL around; a PENINSULA has water on THREE sides; a VALLEY is the low ground between mountains.

Read this:

A map is a drawing of a place from above. To read one you need three tools. The compass rose shows the directions — north, south, east and west. The key (or legend) explains what the little symbols mean. The scale tells you how much real distance a small map distance stands for. Maps also show landforms — natural features like mountains, valleys, islands and peninsulas.

Read this:

The Vikings were seafaring people from Scandinavia — today’s Norway, Sweden and Denmark — about 1,000 years ago. The explorer Leif Erikson reached North America around the year 1000 — about 500 years before Columbus. Their stories were told in long tales called sagas.

How to do it: Big ideas: Ancient China began on the YELLOW RIVER and was ruled by DYNASTIES (ruling families). The GREAT WALL was built for defence. Four famous Chinese inventions: PAPER, SILK, the COMPASS and GUNPOWDER. The SILK ROAD was the trade route that carried those goods — and ideas — all the way to Europe.

Read this:

Ancient China was one of the world’s oldest civilizations, growing along the Yellow River in Asia thousands of years ago. It was ruled by families of emperors called dynasties. To keep out invaders, workers built the enormous Great Wall of China. Chinese inventors gave the world paper, silk, the compass and gunpowder. Traders carried Chinese silk thousands of miles west along a route called the Silk Road, connecting China with distant lands.

🌎 The Maya & the Aztec

WordWhat it is

💡
How to do it: Tell them apart: the MAYA lived in the Central American RAINFOREST, wrote in GLYPHS and built an amazingly accurate CALENDAR. The AZTEC built their capital TENOCHTITLAN on an ISLAND in a lake. What they SHARED: stone PYRAMIDS, skilled farming, and MAIZE (corn) as their key crop.

Read this:

Long before Europeans arrived, great civilizations flourished in the Americas. The Maya lived in the rainforests of Central America. They built stone pyramids, invented a written language of picture symbols called glyphs, and created an incredibly accurate calendar. Further north, the Aztec built a magnificent capital city, Tenochtitlan, on an island in a lake — with causeways, canals and floating gardens. Both peoples were expert farmers who grew maize (corn) as their most important crop.
